clue.text: The challenge of accommodating Aunt Letitia

indicators.note: 'of' here means drawn out of, so the letters are taken from inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: the last letter of accommodating plus the start of the two names

explanation.surface: Someone has the trying task of putting up a visiting aunt called Letitia.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts on the final G of accommodating, a word that also pretends to be the signal for something going inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw down the gauntlet is to issue a challenge, so the glove itself stands for the challenge by figurative extension.

clue.text: Newspaperman gets half inch

indicators.note: only half of the preceding word is kept, its second two letters being dropped

blocks.note: ED is short for editor, the newspaperman in charge
taken as written before it is cut down

explanation.surface: A journalist ends up with only half an inch of column space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half inch' reads as a measurement, but 'half' works on gets and inch is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To inch forward and to edge forward both describe moving slowly and carefully, a little at a time.

clue.text: Doctor in middle of walk makes sacrifice

indicators.note: placing one thing in the middle of another means putting it inside

blocks.note: a gait is a manner of walking
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A physician wanders into the middle of a stroll and gives something up.
explanation.walkthrough: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is the usual crossword doctor; walk is a noun here, a way of walking, not a stroll.
explanation.definitionFit: A gambit is a chess opening in which a player sacrifices a piece to gain an advantage.

clue.text: Extra food for boxers' helpers

blocks.note: first meaning: a further helping at a meal
second meaning: the attendants in a boxer's corner

explanation.surface: A boxer's corner team is fed a little more at mealtime.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking for another serving is asking for more helpings, and the assistants who attend a boxer between rounds are called by the same name.

clue.text: Scrap a lot of money? That makes a big bang

blocks.note: an atom is a tiny scrap, as in not an atom of truth
a bomb is British slang for a large sum, as in costing a bomb

explanation.surface: Throwing away a fortune, the speaker suggests, would cause an uproar.
explanation.walkthrough: Scrap looks like a verb meaning discard, but it is a noun for a tiny piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuclear weapon of the fission kind produces a vast explosion, which is described playfully here.

clue.text: Counter-plot calls for telegram security equipment

blocks.note: a bar is the counter of a pub
a garden bed is a plot for flowers
a wire is an old word for a telegram

explanation.surface: A conspiracy to foil another plot needs urgent cabled messages and some protective gear.
explanation.definitionFit: Fencing strung with sharp points is used around sites to keep intruders out, a classic protective barrier.

clue.text: Swanson impregnates rag with oil

indicators.note: to impregnate is to soak one substance right through another, so the letters are thoroughly mixed together

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone called Swanson soaks a cloth in oil.
explanation.walkthrough: Swanson is the surname of the Hollywood star of Sunset Boulevard, so the clue asks for her first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The silent-film and Sunset Boulevard actress Gloria Swanson is the famous bearer of this surname, so it identifies her first name.

clue.text: Poisonous plant disposes of servant and Sir Francis

blocks.note: a man is a manservant
Sir Francis Drake, the Elizabethan seafarer

explanation.surface: A toxic plant kills off a servant and the famous Elizabethan admiral.
explanation.definitionFit: The forked root of this Mediterranean herb is toxic and was long credited with magical, narcotic powers.

clue.text: Follows storyteller in street going westwards

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another is placed inside it
in an across entry, travelling west means reading from right to left

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
a liar tells stories, in the sense of untruths

explanation.surface: Someone tails a teller of tales heading west along a road.
explanation.walkthrough: S-LIAR-T read backwards. Storyteller suggests an author, but a story here is a fib.
explanation.definitionFit: To trail someone is to follow behind them, so the third-person verb matches.

clue.text: Stake where Italian poet lost his head

indicators.note: losing a head means the first letter of the named poet is taken away

blocks.note: Dante Alighieri, author of the Divine Comedy

explanation.surface: A betting stake is placed where an Italian poet was beheaded.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker the opening bet each player puts into the pot before the deal is a stake of this kind.

clue.text: Literary group flourishes next to sink

blocks.note: a plant that flourishes blooms
to sink something is to bury it

explanation.surface: A writers' circle thrives beside the kitchen basin.
explanation.walkthrough: Sink looks like a noun for a basin, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Virginia Woolf, E. M. Forster and friends were named the Bloomsbury Group after the London district where they met.

clue.text: Dimwit absorbs Stock Exchange secret

indicators.note: to absorb something is to take it inside oneself

blocks.note: a clot is British slang for a fool
SE is the abbreviation for Stock Exchange

explanation.surface: A fool soaks up a confidential tip from the City's trading floor.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, a closet supporter is a hidden or private one, kept out of public view.

clue.text: It resolves difficulties in an isolated village

blocks.note: first meaning: an agreement ending a dispute
second meaning: a small community, often remote

explanation.surface: A remote village is where some trouble gets sorted out.
explanation.definitionFit: An agreed deal that ends a legal dispute and a newly founded community in remote country share the same name.

clue.text: Shut up shed and flat

blocks.note: to shed something is to drop it, as leaves are dropped
a flat battery is a dead one

explanation.surface: Someone locks up the garden hut and the apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: Shut up looks like locking the shed; it is the rude dismissal, and shed and flat are not buildings.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are rude, dismissive exclamations telling someone to go away and stop talking.

clue.text: Making endless noise about rubbish, backing Victoria?

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off
going backwards means the letters are read from the end
about means placed around something else

blocks.note: taken as written before it is trimmed
tat is cheap, tasteless junk

explanation.surface: Someone endlessly complains about rubbish while supporting a woman named Victoria.
explanation.walkthrough: NOIS turns into SION, which wraps TAT after its S. The question mark warns that Victoria is an example, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: London Victoria is a major railway terminus, so the name is an example of a railway stop.

clue.text: Death sentences?

blocks.note: surface reading: judicial verdicts condemning someone to execution
setter's reading: sentences of prose written about someone who has died

explanation.walkthrough: A sentence can be a judge's penalty or a line of written prose; the question mark flags the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper notice reporting a death and summing up the life is written in sentences about that death.

clue.text: One attracted to card game shows how to cut

blocks.note: A means one, as in a single thing
bridge is a partnership card game

explanation.surface: A keen player of a card game demonstrates how to cut the pack.
explanation.walkthrough: Cut suggests cutting cards; it means shorten a text.
explanation.definitionFit: To shorten a book or speech while keeping its sense is to condense it, the verb asked for.

clue.text: Keeper of hardy animals is an unlikely dog-hater

indicators.note: something unlikely is improbable, so the letters must be rearranged into a more plausible form

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the hyphen

explanation.surface: A shepherd of tough beasts would hardly hate the sheepdog.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that a herder relies on dogs, so a dog-hater makes an unlikely one.
explanation.definitionFit: Goats are famously hardy animals, and someone who tends a herd of them is their keeper.

clue.text: Apprentice journalist caught up in dangerous feat

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom
something caught in another thing is held inside it

blocks.note: a stunt is a daring, risky feat
ED, editor, is the crossword's usual journalist

explanation.surface: A trainee reporter gets caught up in a risky stunt.
explanation.definitionFit: An apprentice and a learner at college are both people still being taught a trade or subject, broad synonyms.

clue.text: Slug with tail squashed by French politician

indicators.note: squashed things are crushed out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A French politician steps on a slug, tail and all.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of Charles de Gaulle's conservative nationalist movement in France is a politician of that tradition.

clue.text: Coldness of a course unknown

blocks.note: taken as written
a path is a course or route
Y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Someone's chilly manner about a route nobody knows.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of interest or feeling toward things is a kind of indifference, emotional chilliness.

clue.text: Deposit secures little back room for manoeuvre

indicators.note: back means the preceding word is read in the opposite direction
to secure something is to hold it fast inside

blocks.note: to lay something down is to deposit it
wee is Scottish for little

explanation.surface: A down payment secures a small back room that gives some flexibility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back room' reads as one phrase; back belongs to little, and room starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeway is the margin of freedom or slack available to act, the space you have to move around in.

clue.text: Untrained person writing short poem on staff

blocks.note: a lay is a short narrative poem or song
to staff a desk is to man it

explanation.surface: An amateur pens a little verse about the office workforce.
explanation.walkthrough: Staff looks like a noun for employees, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-professional without specialist training in a field is one of the lay public, not an expert.

clue.text: Fix up my sandal for this religious festival

indicators.note: to fix something can mean to rework or rig it, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks for their sandal to be repaired in time for a church holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fix up' reads as a phrasal verb meaning repair, but up is part of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sunday before Easter celebrates Christ's entry to Jerusalem, when crowds waved fronds, a Christian feast day.

clue.text: The pain borne by Rachel

indicators.note: something borne by a word is carried inside it

blocks.note: the middle letters of the name

explanation.surface: A woman named Rachel suffers in silence.
explanation.definitionFit: A dull continuous hurt in part of the body is a kind of soreness, a close synonym.

clue.text: Processed peas found in church

definitions.note: the answer is a part of a church, not the whole building

indicators.note: processed food is broken down and reformed, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Tinned peas turn up in a church.
explanation.definitionFit: The semicircular recess at the east end of a church, often vaulted, is an architectural feature of the building.

clue.text: Polish king - Old Black Eye

blocks.note: to polish shoes is to shine them
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A Polish king was nicknamed Old Black Eye.
explanation.walkthrough: Polish looks like the nationality, with its capital letter, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A bruised, darkened eye from a punch is called this in informal, somewhat dated slang.

clue.text: Turn round headlong in new wooden rescue boat

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way, so it is read backwards
one thing in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for new
oak is a wood, so an oak table is a wooden one
a headlong decision is a rash one

explanation.surface: A wooden lifeboat swings round in a reckless new direction.
explanation.walkthrough: Wooden is read as the timber that something is made of, not its stiff manner.
explanation.definitionFit: The vessel built to save Noah's family and the animals from the Flood was a lifeboat of biblical scale.
